name: New York
note: First in the nation. The bill was watered down from earlier versions (workers' comp was stripped), but it became the legislative template every state that followed adapted.

name: Hawaii
note: Second state in the nation. Hawaii's legislature had Democratic supermajorities in both chambers. Brought domestic workers formally under the state employer-employee framework for the first time.

name: California
note: Brown had vetoed a broader earlier version (AB 889) in 2012. AB 241 was narrower, focused on overtime for personal attendants. A sunset clause was later removed by SB 1015 (2016), making it permanent.

name: Massachusetts
note: Among the broadest bipartisan votes of any DWBR, with over 80 co-sponsors. Patrick was in his final year as governor. Unusually strong rest-period and parental leave provisions, rare among DWBR laws at the time.

name: Connecticut
note: The strongest bipartisan margins of any state DWBR. The final bill was narrowed during negotiation, with overtime and paid sick leave stripped, but anti-discrimination and harassment protections passed with near-unanimous support.

name: Oregon
note: Brown, the first openly bisexual governor in U.S. history, had recently succeeded Gov. Kitzhaber who resigned in February 2015. Oregon's law has the most specific live-in worker rest and sleep provisions of any state DWBR.

name: Illinois
note: The only Republican governor to sign a DWBR. Rauner frequently clashed with the Democratic-controlled legislature, making his signature notable. The law covered approximately 35,000 domestic workers and was among the first to explicitly list military service as a protected characteristic.

name: Nevada
note: One of two Republican governors to sign a DWBR. The Senate passed it on a strict party-line vote with every Republican opposed, yet Sandoval, a noted moderate, signed it anyway. Among the strongest privacy provisions of any state law: employers may not monitor private communications or confiscate personal documents.

name: Seattle
note: First city DWBR in the nation. Sponsored by Councilmember Teresa Mosqueda. Established the first Domestic Workers Standards Board of any city. It became the organizing model Washington would follow eight years later.

name: New Mexico
note: Lujan Grisham's first year as governor. The bill removed the domestic worker exemption from New Mexico's minimum wage law, closing a longstanding loophole that had left workers with no legal recourse.

name: Philadelphia
note: First ordinance to allow paid leave to accrue across multiple employers, directly addressing how domestic work is actually structured. Effective May 1, 2020. Covered an estimated 16,000 workers.

name: Virginia
note: First Southern state to pass a DWBR. Sponsored by Sen. Jennifer McClellan, the first Black woman to represent Richmond in the state Senate. Northam signed it in the final hours before a midnight deadline on near party-line votes.

name: District of Columbia
note: Bowser allowed the bill to lapse into law without signing, reportedly objecting to its funding requirements. The only DWBR whose executive withheld their signature. The DC Council passed it unanimously. Effective October 1, 2023.

name: New Jersey
note: Most comprehensive inclusion of domestic workers in state insurance and benefits systems of any DWBR to date. Murphy signed it four days after Assembly passage. No Republican co-sponsors. Effective July 1, 2024.

name: Rhode Island
note: Eliminated the domestic worker exemption from Rhode Island's Minimum Wage Act. Scope was limited: workers' compensation benefits were not extended. McKee was in his final year as governor.

name: Washington
note: The thirteenth state, and the culmination of Seattle's eight-year proving ground. Ferguson succeeded Jay Inslee. Sponsored by Rep. Brianna Thomas and Sen. Rebecca Saldaña, both from Seattle. See Chapter III for the full legislative timeline.
